## Learning outcomes

By the end of this seminar, you should be able to:

1. **Derive** a fixed-point update from a nonlinear equation, keeping track of its domain.
2. **Calculate** successive iterates and the original residual by hand, using a calculator for arithmetic.
3. **Predict** local convergence or departure using the slope of $g(v)$ and a cobweb sketch.
4. **Check** an apparent solution using both the change between iterates and the original equation.

## Return to the CO₂ equation

What molar volume can CO₂ occupy at a specified temperature and pressure? We have seen this question several times in Lectures 5–7. Some numerical methods are easier to carry out than others. **Fixed-point iteration** needs only a piece of paper, a pen, and a calculator!

::: {.callout-warning}
## Easy to calculate, trickier to converge

An update can be simple to evaluate and still move away from a solution. Revisit the [local slope test and Lipschitz condition in Lecture 6](../../units/02/L06/index.qmd#when-does-fixed-point-iteration-converge). Our choice of $g(v)$ and starting value both matter.
:::

We will work through the algebra and a short iteration table on paper. Keep at least **four significant digits** in intermediate values. Reuse the full calculator display when possible, and round when recording your table. Use these values:

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---:|
| Temperature, $T$ | $280\ \mathrm{K}$ |
| Imposed pressure, $P$ | $50\ \mathrm{bar}$ |
| vdW parameter, $a$ | $3.592\ \mathrm{L^2\,bar\,mol^{-2}}$ |
| vdW parameter, $b$ | $0.04267\ \mathrm{L\,mol^{-1}}$ |
| Gas constant, $R$ | $0.08314462618\ \mathrm{L\,bar\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ |

Using the molar volume $v=V/n$, the van der Waals pressure and its residual function are

$$
P_{\mathrm{EOS}}(v)=\frac{RT}{v-b}-\frac{a}{v^2},
\qquad
\boxed{F(v)=\frac{RT}{v-b}-\frac{a}{v^2}-P.}
$$

Use litres and bar throughout; the physical domain is $v>b$.

A solution has $F(v)=0$: the pressure predicted by the equation matches the imposed pressure. A positive residual means that the predicted pressure is too high.

**Before calculating:** what does $F(v)=0.5\ \mathrm{bar}$ tell you? Does it mean that the volume error is $0.5\ \mathrm{L/mol}$?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check the meaning of the residual

The predicted pressure is $0.5\ \mathrm{bar}$ above the imposed pressure. The residual is a **pressure mismatch**; the volume error would have units of L/mol.
:::


## From an equation to an update

### What is a fixed point?

Suppose a function $g$ takes the current estimate and returns the next one:

$$
v_0\ \longrightarrow\ v_1=g(v_0)\ \longrightarrow\ v_2=g(v_1)\ \longrightarrow\ \cdots.
$$

We write this as

$$
\boxed{v_{k+1}=g(v_k).}
$$

The subscript $k$ counts updates. A **fixed point** $v_s$ satisfies $g(v_s)=v_s$: applying the update leaves that value unchanged. If the sequence converges and $g$ is continuous at its limit, that limit must be a fixed point.

Our job is to choose $g$ so that its fixed points solve the original equation, then check whether repeated updates approach one of them. In [Lecture 6](../../units/02/L06/index.qmd#how-do-we-construct-the-iteration), we used two ways to construct $g$:

1. Set $g(v)=v-c(v)F(v)$, choosing $c(v)$ to be finite and nonzero throughout the domain of interest. Then $g(v_s)=v_s$ is equivalent to $F(v_s)=0$.
2. Rearrange $F(v)=0$ into the form $v=g(v)$, checking the domain of each algebraic step.

For a continuously differentiable $g$, the condition $|g'(v_s)|<1$ gives convergence from sufficiently nearby starting values. We will use the second construction in today's whiteboard derivation.

### Derive $g(v)$ by rearrangement

Start with the pressure equation and isolate $v-b$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{RT}{v-b}-\frac{a}{v^2}&=P,\\[4pt]
\frac{RT}{v-b}&=P+\frac{a}{v^2},\\[4pt]
v-b&=\frac{RT}{P+a/v^2},\\[4pt]
v&=b+\frac{RT}{P+a/v^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Use the current estimate on the right to calculate the next estimate:

$$
\boxed{v_{k+1}=g(v_k)=b+\frac{RT}{P+a/v_k^2}.}
$$

For our positive parameters and $v_k>b$, the denominator is positive and $g(v_k)>b$. Every update therefore stays in the physical domain.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check the reverse algebra

For $v_s>b>0$,

$$
v_s-b=\frac{RT}{P+a/v_s^2}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{RT}{v_s-b}=P+\frac{a}{v_s^2}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
F(v_s)=0.
$$

Reversing the algebra gives the original equation. Every fixed point in the physical domain solves $F(v)=0$; we still need to check whether the iteration reaches one.
:::

### Work through the updates

Once we have $g(v)$, a calculator can carry out each update. Enter a trial volume, record the result, and use that result as the next input.

**How do we choose the first value?** The ideal-gas equation gives a starting estimate:

$$
v_0=\frac{RT}{P}\approx0.4656\ \mathrm{L/mol}.
$$

The calculator below performs **one update**. It displays the new volume, the step, and the original pressure residual. To continue, copy the new volume into the input yourself. The parameters and `g(v)` are visible so you can change the calculation later.

::: {.quarto-wasm-local notebook="s03_fixed_point_calculator.edit.py" view="edit" title="Calculate one fixed-point update for the CO₂ molar volume" height="720" loading="lazy" fullscreen="true"}
**Calculator fallback.** Use $g(v)=0.04267+RT/(50+3.592/v^2)$. From the ideal-gas estimate, one update gives $v_1\approx0.3924\ \mathrm{L/mol}$, a step of $0.07322\ \mathrm{L/mol}$, and a residual of $-6.760\ \mathrm{bar}$. The worked calculation follows.
:::

The first update is

$$
\begin{aligned}
v_1
&=b+\frac{RT}{P+a/v_0^2}\\[4pt]
&\approx0.04267+\frac{23.28}{66.57}\\[4pt]
&\approx0.3924\ \mathrm{L/mol}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Now check this **new** volume in the original equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
F(v_1)
&=\frac{RT}{v_1-0.04267}-\frac{3.592}{v_1^2}-50\\[4pt]
&\approx-6.760\ \mathrm{bar}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The initial residual was $F(v_0)\approx-11.52\ \mathrm{bar}$. One update has reduced its magnitude to about $6.760\ \mathrm{bar}$. The predicted pressure is still below the imposed pressure.

## When should we stop?

For this hand exercise, use the deliberately coarse tolerances

$$
\varepsilon_v=0.001\ \mathrm{L/mol},
\qquad
\varepsilon_P=0.2\ \mathrm{bar}.
$$

Accept an iterate when **both** conditions hold:

$$
\boxed{
|v_k-v_{k-1}|<\varepsilon_v
\quad\text{and}\quad
|F(v_k)|<\varepsilon_P.
}
$$

**Your turn:** which row first passes both checks? Which row would you accept too early if you checked only the step?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check the stopping decision

At $k=11$, the step is about $0.0009468\ \mathrm{L/mol}$, which passes the volume-step tolerance. The residual magnitude is still about $0.2289\ \mathrm{bar}$, which fails the pressure tolerance.

At $k=12$, both checks pass. We can report $v\approx0.3086\ \mathrm{L/mol}$ with a pressure residual of about $-0.17\ \mathrm{bar}$ under the stated stopping rule. Tighter tolerances require more updates.

The step tolerance measures the change between successive estimates. The actual volume error $|v_k-v_s|$ at $k=12$ is still about $0.002002\ \mathrm{L/mol}$, larger than $\varepsilon_v$.
:::

A practical calculation should also check that each value is finite and remains in the physical domain. Reaching a maximum iteration count without meeting the tolerances should produce a failure report.

### Try a constant $c$

Return to the other construction from Lecture 6:

$$
g_c(v)=v-cF(v),
\qquad c=-0.01000\ \mathrm{L\,mol^{-1}\,bar^{-1}}.
$$

The units of $c$ turn the pressure residual into a volume correction. Since $c\ne0$, a fixed point of this choice of $g$ solves $F(v)=0$.

Replace `g(v)` in the calculator with:

```{.python code-fold="false"}
def g(v):
    c = -0.01  # L / (mol bar)
    return v - c * F(v)
```

Start again from the ideal-gas estimate. Enter each new volume manually and record the step and residual. How many updates are needed before both stopping checks pass? Then try `c = -0.02`. Does the approach stay on one side of the root or alternate?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check the constant-$c$ calculation

For $c=-0.01$, the first update gives $v_1\approx0.3504\ \mathrm{L/mol}$ and $F(v_1)\approx-3.601\ \mathrm{bar}$. Both stopping checks first pass at $k=5$, with $v_5\approx0.3066\ \mathrm{L/mol}$.

Near the gas-like root, $g_c'(v_s)=1-cF'(v_s)$ is about $0.1505$ for $c=-0.01$ and $-0.6991$ for $c=-0.02$. The first choice approaches from one side; the second alternates. These signs and magnitudes explain what you should see in your calculations.
:::

## Why does the rearrangement matter?

### The slope tells us what happens to a nearby error

At a fixed point, the graphs of $y=g(v)$ and $y=v$ intersect. Imagine starting a little to one side of that intersection. Does one update bring you closer or push you farther away?

For a continuously differentiable $g(v)$ near $v_s$, the local rule is:

| Slope at the fixed point | Expected behaviour for sufficiently nearby starts |
|---|---|
| $0<g'(v_s)<1$ | Errors shrink and keep their sign |
| $-1<g'(v_s)<0$ | Errors shrink and alternate in sign |
| $|g'(v_s)|>1$ | The fixed point repels nearby errors |
| $g'(v_s)=0$ | Locally attracting; higher-order terms control the error |
| $|g'(v_s)|=1$ | This slope test is inconclusive |

A slope of $0.75$, for example, means that a small error becomes about three quarters as large after one update. This is a **local** test. A starting point far away may behave differently.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hand derivation: the error after one update

Define the signed error $e_k=v_k-v_s$. Since $v_s=g(v_s)$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
e_{k+1}
&=g(v_k)-g(v_s)\\
&=g(v_s+e_k)-g(v_s)\\
&\approx g'(v_s)e_k.
\end{aligned}
$$

The last line uses the tangent-line approximation near $v_s$. Taking absolute values gives

$$
|e_{k+1}|\approx|g'(v_s)|\,|e_k|.
$$

This explains why the magnitude of the slope controls whether a small error shrinks, while its sign controls whether the error changes sign.

For our first choice of $g(v)$, differentiate after writing the fraction without $v^{-2}$:

$$
g(v)=b+\frac{RTv^2}{Pv^2+a}.
$$

The quotient rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
g'(v)
&=RT\frac{2v(Pv^2+a)-v^2(2Pv)}{(Pv^2+a)^2}\\[4pt]
&=\boxed{\frac{2aRTv}{(Pv^2+a)^2}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

At the gas-like root $v_s\approx0.3065501\ \mathrm{L/mol}$,

$$
g'(v_s)\approx0.7459.
$$

It is positive and below one, consistent with the approach from above in our table. You may use the supplied root to check the slope; the iteration itself does not need the root in advance.
:::

### Sketch two cobweb steps

On paper, label the horizontal axis $v$ and the vertical axis $y$, both in L/mol. Sketch $y=v$ and the increasing curve $y=g(v)$ over $0.30$–$0.47\ \mathrm{L/mol}$ so that your first two updates fit. They intersect near $0.3066\ \mathrm{L/mol}$. The slope of $g$ at that intersection is about $0.746$, so it crosses the diagonal less steeply.

1. Start at $(v_0,v_0)$ on the diagonal.
2. Move vertically to $(v_0,g(v_0))=(v_0,v_1)$ on the curve.
3. Move horizontally to $(v_1,v_1)$ on the diagonal.
4. Repeat with $v_1$ to reach $(v_1,v_2)$, then $(v_2,v_2)$.

Use the values in your table to label the first two steps. The horizontal move puts the new value in position to become the next input.

**Discuss:** do these steps approach the intersection from one side or cross back and forth? How would the sketch change if the slope near the intersection were $-0.75$?

### A second rearrangement of the same equation

This time, isolate the attraction term:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{a}{v^2}&=\frac{RT}{v-b}-P,\\[4pt]
v^2&=\frac{a}{RT/(v-b)-P}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Since physical molar volumes are positive, take the positive square root:

$$
\boxed{v_{k+1}=h(v_k)=\sqrt{\frac{a}{RT/(v_k-b)-P}}.}
$$

This choice of $h(v)$ needs a positive denominator. With our parameters, its physical input domain is

$$
b<v_k<b+\frac{RT}{P}\approx0.50828\ \mathrm{L/mol}.
$$

An update can leave this interval, so the domain must be checked again before the next update.

**Your turn:** start again from the ideal-gas estimate $v_0\approx0.4656\ \mathrm{L/mol}$ and calculate one update. Does it move toward the gas-like root near $0.3066\ \mathrm{L/mol}$? Can you use the result as the next input?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check the second rearrangement

The first update gives

$$
v_1\approx0.8438\ \mathrm{L/mol},
\qquad F(v_1)\approx-25.99\ \mathrm{bar}.
$$

This moves away from the gas-like root and exceeds the upper input limit $b+RT/P\approx0.5083\ \mathrm{L/mol}$. The next update would take the square root of a negative number, so we must stop.

At the gas-like root,

$$
h'(v_s)\approx1.341>1.
$$

The same root satisfies $h(v_s)=v_s$, but this choice repels sufficiently nearby iterates. Our ideal-gas start also fails, as the direct domain check shows.
:::

Both rearrangements describe the same physical roots within their domains. Their updates behave differently because our choices of $g(v)$ and $h(v)$ have different slopes.

## Fixed-point iteration before calculators

Repeated updating long predates calculators and Python. Its simple arithmetic also makes it suitable for pen-and-paper questions in an engineering exam.

How long is the diagonal of a square with side length one? Pythagoras gives $x^2=2$, so the positive length is $\sqrt{2}$. To approximate it, **Heron's method** repeatedly averages an estimate $x$ with $2/x$. Heron of Alexandria described this square-root procedure in the first century CE; related methods were already known to the Babylonians ([MacTutor biography](https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Heron/)). In today's notation, it is a fixed-point iteration:

$$
\boxed{x_{k+1}=g_H(x_k)=\frac12\left(x_k+\frac{2}{x_k}\right),\qquad x_k>0.}
$$

Check that its positive fixed point solves $f(x)=x^2-2=0$:

$$
x_s=\frac12\left(x_s+\frac{2}{x_s}\right)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
2x_s^2=x_s^2+2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
x_s^2=2.
$$

### A Newton–Raphson point of view

Heron's method is Newton–Raphson applied to $f(x)=x^2-2$:

$$
x_{k+1}=x_k-\frac{x_k^2-2}{2x_k}
=\frac12\left(x_k+\frac{2}{x_k}\right).
$$

Starting from $x_0=1$, just three updates give $x_3\approx1.414216$. The rapid local convergence we discussed in Lecture 6 explains how a few arithmetic steps can give such an accurate square-root approximation.

## Before you leave

Can you use fixed-point iteration to approach the other two CO₂ roots? Try starting near $0.08767$ and $0.1141\ \mathrm{L/mol}$. Does the same choice of $g(v)$ work for both? Use its slope and the original residual to explain what happens.
